analysis.one_liner: Requires courts to judge federal agencies' legal interpretations fresh, without deferring to the agency.
analysis.headline: A Republican bill to strip courts' automatic deference to federal agency legal interpretations died in the House Judiciary Committee with 21 supporters and never reached a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Under current law (known as Chevron deference), when a federal law is ambiguous, courts usually accept the agency's own reading of it. This bill would change the Administrative Procedure Act so judges reviewing an agency action must decide all questions of law "de novo" — from scratch, giving no weight to the agency's interpretation — and would apply that rule to every judicial review of agency action unless a law specifically exempts it. That would make agency rules and decisions easier to overturn in court. The bill never advanced past referral to a Judiciary subcommittee.
analysis.who_benefits: Regulated industries — companies subject to environmental, workplace, financial, drug-safety, and other federal rules — gain a powerful litigation tool: any rule they oppose could be re-litigated on the merits of its legal interpretation, with a judge free to disagree with the agency. Challengers of agency decisions in immigration, benefits, and enforcement cases also gain a fresh chance to argue the law means something else.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Companies that challenge federal regulations in court

how_it_helps.text: The bill amends the Administrative Procedure Act so that a reviewing court must "decide de novo all relevant questions of law," including the meaning of constitutional provisions, statutes, and agency rules — that is, without giving any deference to the agency's own interpretation.

It would apply this no-deference standard to every civil action reviewing agency action under any law, and no other law could exempt a case from the standard except by specifically referencing this section.

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary people who depend on federal agencies to interpret and enforce protections — clean air and water rules, workplace safety standards, consumer and drug safety, and benefit programs — would bear the cost when courts substitute their own readings for expert agencies' and more rules are struck down or delayed. Agencies would also face more litigation over every interpretation.
analysis.who_pays_short: People relying on federal agency protections

drawbacks.text: De novo review lets unelected judges substitute their own legal judgments for those of career agency experts whenever a statute is ambiguous, which can make major protections more vulnerable to being narrowed or struck down by courts.

The bill would apply automatically to every judicial review of agency action and could only be overridden law-by-law with specific reference to the section, so the change sweeps far beyond any single agency or rule and would sharply increase litigation over agency interpretations.

Supporters' strongest argument — that letting agencies interpret ambiguous laws they enforce concentrates too much power in the executive branch and that judges, not agencies, should say what the law is — is a genuine constitutional position, not just an industry talking point; the counterweight is that agency expertise and political accountability exist precisely to fill gaps Congress left open.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targets a real constitutional debate — whether agencies or courts should settle ambiguous law. But its effect would fall unevenly: the parties most able to exploit fresh judicial review are well-funded companies challenging rules they dislike, while the public benefits from stable, expert interpretation of health, safety, and environmental laws. On balance, its main practical effect would be to make federal regulation easier to unwind in court.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and then to its antitrust and administrative-law subcommittee, where it sat with no markup, no committee vote, and no floor vote until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative John Ratcliffe introduced the bill on March 27, 2019, joined by 20 Republican cosponsors.
The House referred it to the Judiciary Committee on the day of introduction, and on May 3, 2019, to the Subcommittee on Antitrust, Commercial, and Administrative Law.
No further action appears in the record: the bill never received a subcommittee or committee vote and never reached the House floor before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Federal agencies keep their interpretive authority — under current law courts still defer to reasonable agency readings of ambiguous statutes — so the health, safety, environmental, and consumer protections that depend on that deference remain intact, and regulated industries did not get the new litigation tool this bill would have handed them.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Agencies and the protections they enforce

for.name: Rep. John Ratcliffe
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to require de novo judicial review of agency legal interpretations.

for.name: 20 of 197 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction; all 20 cosponsors were Republicans.

against.name: Rep. Jerrold Nadler
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a committee markup; after subcommittee referral in May 2019, no committee action occurred for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all 20 cosponsors were Republicans in a Democratic-controlled House; the Democratic Judiciary chair never brought it to a vote, and no Democrat appears anywhere in the record as a supporter.

industries.industry: Regulated industries (energy, pharmaceutical, financial, and other companies subject to federal rules)
industries.note: If passed, the bill would have given these companies a new way to overturn federal rules: a judge re-deciding the law from scratch instead of deferring to the agency. Their gain would come at the cost of weaker, less predictable health, safety, and environmental protections for the public.

industries.industry: Federal regulatory agencies (EPA, OSHA, FDA, financial regulators, and others)
industries.note: Agencies would lose the judicial deference that lets their expert interpretations of ambiguous statutes stand, exposing nearly every rule and enforcement decision to fresh legal challenge. That loss falls on the agencies that administer protections ordinary people rely on.
